MSK__Joint Pain:
Joint pain (arthralgia) is one of the commonest presenting symptoms — and the trick is a structured sort before you reach for tests. Ask four questions. (1) Articular or periarticular? — is the joint itself painful (pain on all movement, effusion, deep/diffuse) or a tendon / bursa / bone around it (point tenderness, pain on one movement)? (2) Inflammatory or mechanical? — inflammatory = early-morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, swelling / warmth / erythema, night pain, systemic upset; mechanical / degenerative = worse through the day / with use, stiffness <30 min, better with rest. (3) What pattern? — mono (1) vs oligo (2–4) vs poly (≥5), symmetry, large vs small, axial vs peripheral, migratory vs additive (see monoarthritis, polyarthritis). (4) Acute or chronic?
🚨A single acute hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate the joint (before antibiotics if possible) and do not delay (see hot swollen joint, bone & joint infection). Also flagged: fever with systemic upset, joint pain with a rash / photosensitivity, oral ulcers or red eye (connective tissue disease / spondyloarthropathy), new inflammatory arthritis with weight loss or night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis), and any joint pain after trauma (fracture).

1Recognise & sort
🔍Take the pain apart
  • Articular (pain on all movement, effusion) vs periarticular (point tenderness, pain on one specific movement — tendon / bursa)
  • Inflammatory (morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, hot / swollen, night pain) vs mechanical (worse with use, stiffness <30 min, eases with rest)
  • Define onset (acute vs chronic), number of joints, symmetry, and whether it is migratory or additive
🚩Red-flag patterns
  • Single acute hot swollen joint → septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate (see joint infection)
  • Fever / systemic upset, or arthritis with a rash, oral ulcers, red eye or new murmur (CTD, spondyloarthropathy, endocarditis)
  • New inflammatory arthritis + weight loss / night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis); any post-traumatic joint pain (fracture)
🔵Acute patterns
  • Acute monoarthritis: septic arthritis, gout / pseudogout (see crystal arthropathy), haemarthrosis, trauma
  • Migratory (moves joint to joint): gonococcal, rheumatic fever, viral, Lyme, early connective tissue disease
  • Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis: viral (e.g. parvovirus), early rheumatoid arthritis
🟢Chronic patterns
  • Symmetrical small joints (MCP / PIP / wrist), morning stiffness → rheumatoid arthritis (see RA)
  • Asymmetrical large joints / axial + enthesitis / dactylitis → spondyloarthropathy (psoriatic, reactive, axial, IBD-related, see spondyloarthropathy)
  • DIP + weight-bearing joints, worse with use, bony swelling → osteoarthritis (see OA)
🟣Don’t-miss systemic clues
  • Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, Raynaud’s, serositis → connective tissue disease / SLE (see CTD)
  • Psoriasis / nail changes, uveitis, urethritis or recent diarrhoea, IBD → a spondyloarthropathy
  • Widespread pain, tender points, fatigue, non-inflammatory → fibromyalgia (a diagnosis of exclusion, see fibromyalgia)
  • Over-50s, proximal shoulder / pelvic-girdle pain + long morning stiffness, very high ESR → polymyalgia rheumatica (watch for giant cell arteritis)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine with look–feel–move: effusion, warmth, deformity, range; screen the other joints, skin, nails and eyes
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF & anti-CCP, ANA, HLA-B27 (selectively), U&E / LFTs
  • Joint aspiration (MC&S, crystals, Gram — mandatory for a hot joint) and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound / MRI) as guided
Sort before you test. Two questions do most of the work: is it inflammatory or mechanical (the morning-stiffness clock — >30–60 min and easing with use = inflammatory), and how many joints, how symmetrical? Those two axes place most arthritis before a single blood test — and a single hot joint always gets aspirated to exclude sepsis.

MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint:
An acute hot, swollen, painful joint is a finding that carries one overriding rule: it is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and carries a real mortality, so the priority is a diagnostic joint aspiration before you commit to any other label. The differential is short and worth knowing cold: septic arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis (trauma / anticoagulation / bleeding disorder), a reactive arthritis, an acute flare of a known inflammatory arthritis, and trauma / fracture. The one test that separates them is the synovial fluid — Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals (see joint pain, bone & joint infection).
🚨Aspirate the joint URGENTLY, before antibiotics — send fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals, take blood cultures, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for washout (see septic arthritis). Never dismiss a hot joint as “just a gout flare” — sepsis and crystals can coexist. A prosthetic joint must not be tapped at the bedside — refer to orthopaedics for aspiration in theatre.

1Recognise & act
🔍Recognise it
  • Red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint with an effusion, markedly reduced range and held still
  • Ask about fever / systemic upset, speed of onset, prior joint disease, trauma and anticoagulation
  • Note risk factors for sepsis: prosthetic joint, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, immunosuppression, IVDU, a skin breach
🚩The emergency response
  • Septic arthritis until proven otherwise → URGENT aspiration before antibiotics (Gram / culture / crystals / cell count)
  • Take blood cultures + FBC / CRP, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for joint washout (see joint infection)
  • Prosthetic joint → do not aspirate at the bedside; refer to orthopaedics for theatre aspiration
🔵The differential
  • Septic arthritis: Staph aureus commonest; gonococcal in the young / sexually active (migratory, tenosynovitis, pustules)
  • Crystal arthritis: gout (podagra, see gouty tophi) and pseudogout (CPPD, knee / wrist, elderly, see crystal arthropathy)
  • Haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulation, haemophilia), reactive arthritis, and an acute flare of RA / spondyloarthropathy (see RA)
🟢Read the synovial fluid
  • Septic: turbid / purulent, very high WCC (often >50×10⁹/L, >90% neutrophils), organisms on Gram / culture
  • Crystal: negatively birefringent needles = urate (gout); positively birefringent rhomboids = CPPD (pseudogout)
  • Haemarthrosis: frank blood (± fat globules if intra-articular fracture)
🟣Mimics & pitfalls
  • Cellulitis / bursitis can look similar but the joint moves freely and the effusion is outside the joint line
  • A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot (neuropathic) joint, not infection (see neuropathic foot, Charcot joint)
  • Serum urate is often normal or low during an acute gout attack — it does not exclude gout, and a raised urate does not confirm it
🩺Investigate & treat
  • Joint aspiration (the decisive test) + blood cultures, FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, U&E, coagulation
  • Empirical IV antibiotics after aspiration (per local policy, e.g. flucloxacillin) and surgical washout / drainage
  • In a child with a hot hip use the Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12) to weigh septic vs transient synovitis
Tap first, label later. Every acute hot swollen joint is septic until the aspirate says otherwise — so the reflex is arthrocentesis before antibiotics, blood cultures, then empirical IV cover and washout. Gout is the commonest true cause, but you can only call it gout after excluding sepsis, because the two can sit in the same joint.

Urate misleads in the acute attack. A normal or low serum urate does not exclude gout (urate often falls during an attack), and a high urate does not confirm it — the diagnosis is made on crystals in the aspirate under polarised light, having first excluded infection.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — assess, aspirate, culture, treat
Assess the joint & host
Red / hot / swollen / tender, effusion, range, held still; fever; and the sepsis risk factors (prosthesis, RA, diabetes, immunosuppression, IVDU)
Aspirate the joint
Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → Gram stain, culture, cell count, crystals. A prosthetic joint is aspirated in theatre by orthopaedics, not at the bedside
Bloods & cultures
Blood cultures, FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, U&E, coagulation; imaging (X-ray for fracture / chondrocalcinosis, ultrasound to confirm an effusion)
Treat in parallel
If sepsis is possible, start empirical IV antibiotics after the tap and refer for washout; treat crystal disease with NSAID / colchicine / steroid once infection is excluded
Then — confirm on the synovial fluid
Septic arthritis → synovial Gram / culture + high WCCGout → negatively birefringent needlesPseudogout → positively birefringent rhomboidsHaemarthrosis → blood on aspiration + coagulationReactive arthritis → sterile fluid + preceding infection
The rules that carry it: an acute hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics, culture the blood, then treat with IV antibiotics and washout. The synovial fluid (Gram / WCC / crystals) makes the diagnosis; gout and sepsis can coexist, and urate is unreliable in the acute attack.

MSK__Monoarthritis:
Monoarthritis is inflammation of a single joint. The first split is tempo. An acute monoarthritis (days) is a medical emergency — septic arthritis until proven otherwise — and is worked up as a hot joint (see acute hot swollen joint): septic, crystal (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis, reactive or traumatic. A chronic monoarthritis (persisting >6 weeks) opens a different differential that is easy to forget: osteoarthritis, chronic infection (tuberculosis, fungal, Brucella), a monoarticular presentation of RA / a spondyloarthropathy, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour, or avascular necrosis. The unifying move is the same: aspirate the joint — and if it stays undiagnosed, biopsy the synovium (see joint pain).
🚨Any acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics, take blood cultures, and treat (see septic arthritis). Do not be reassured by a “normal” serum urate. For a chronic monoarthritis that resists diagnosis, think tuberculosis and tumour — both need a synovial (or bone) biopsy, not just more blood tests. A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot joint, not sepsis.

1Recognise & split
🔍Split by tempo first
  • Acute (days) → work up as a hot joint — septic, crystal, haemarthrosis, reactive, trauma (see hot joint)
  • Chronic (>6 weeks) → a different list: OA, chronic infection, monoarticular systemic arthritis, PVNS, tumour, AVN
  • Ask about trauma, fever, risk factors, TB exposure, prior joint disease and the speed of onset
🚩Red-flag patterns
  • Acute hot monoarthritis → septic until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics (see joint infection)
  • Chronic mono that resists diagnosis → think TB and tumour — both need a biopsy
  • Rapidly destructive joint / night pain / weight loss → malignancy or chronic sepsis
🔵Acute monoarthritis
  • Septic arthritis (Staph aureus; gonococcal in the young) — the must-exclude
  • Crystal: gout (podagra, see gouty tophi) and pseudogout (CPPD, knee / wrist, elderly, see crystal arthropathy)
  • Haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulation, haemophilia), reactive arthritis, trauma / internal derangement
🟢Chronic monoarthritis (>6 weeks)
  • Osteoarthritis (commonest chronic mono, see OA) and avascular necrosis (see AVN)
  • Chronic infection: tuberculosis, fungal, Brucella, Lyme — indolent, needs synovial biopsy / culture
  • Monoarticular presentation of RA / psoriatic / spondyloarthropathy (see RA, spondyloarthropathy), PVNS, or tumour (see bone tumour)
🟣Clues & pitfalls
  • PVNS: a recurrent blood-stained effusion in a young adult knee (a benign proliferative synovial tumour)
  • Haemochromatosis arthropathy favours the 2nd / 3rd MCP joints with hook osteophytes (usually more than one joint)
  • A normal or low serum urate does not exclude gout; a “flare” that will not settle should be re-aspirated
🩺Investigate
  • Aspirate every case — Gram / culture (incl. TB / fungal if chronic), cell count, crystals; blood cultures if acute
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF / anti-CCP, ANA, HLA-B27 selectively, ferritin (haemochromatosis)
  • Imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, MRI); if a chronic mono stays undiagnosed → synovial biopsy (TB, PVNS, tumour)
Tempo picks the differential. Acute monoarthritis is a hot-joint emergency (septic until proven otherwise); chronic monoarthritis (>6 weeks) is a different list topped by osteoarthritis, TB and tumour. Both start with a joint aspiration — and the chronic, undiagnosed joint ends with a synovial biopsy.

Don’t forget TB and PVNS. A chronic, cool-ish, single swollen joint that does not fit crystal or OA — especially a knee with a recurrent haemorrhagic effusion (PVNS) or an indolent joint in someone with TB risk — is the classic trap. The answer is nearly always a synovial biopsy.

At the bedside — split by tempo, aspirate, image
Split by tempo
Acute (days) = hot-joint emergency; chronic (>6 weeks) = OA / TB / PVNS / tumour / AVN. Ask about trauma, fever, TB exposure and prior joint disease
Aspirate the joint
Arthrocentesis in every case — Gram / culture (add TB & fungal if chronic), cell count, crystals; blood cultures if acute (see hot joint)
Blood & imaging
FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF / anti-CCP, ANA, ferritin; X-ray, ultrasound, MRI (AVN, PVNS, tumour, chondrocalcinosis)
Biopsy if undiagnosed
A chronic monoarthritis that remains undiagnosed after aspiration → synovial biopsy for histology and TB / fungal culture
Then — confirm the cause
Septic arthritis → synovial Gram / cultureCrystal arthritis → polarised-light crystalsTuberculous arthritis → synovial biopsy + TB culturePVNS → MRI + synovial biopsyAvascular necrosis → MRI of the joint
The rules that carry it: classify a monoarthritis by tempo — acute is a septic emergency (aspirate before antibiotics), chronic (>6 weeks) is OA / TB / PVNS / tumour / AVN. Aspirate everyone; biopsy the synovium when a chronic joint stays undiagnosed.
